title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. When a market prices a record backlog at an average multiple, it is usually doubting either the margin or the delivery clock.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Maxim

web_blocks.html: At the November 18, 2026 close of $348.26, GD carries an equity market cap of $94.11 billion and enterprise value of $98.71 billion [13][14]. On trailing results, the stock trades at 20.48x P/E ($17.01 TTM diluted EPS) and 18.43x Forward P/E [13][14]. It also trades at 14.50x EV/EBITDA, 1.75x EV/Sales, and 16.28x Price-to-Free-Cash-Flow (a 6.14% trailing FCF yield), with a 1.80% dividend yield ($6.27 TTM) [13][14]. Across its 10-year history, GD typically traded between 15x and 21x forward earnings. Today's 18.43x forward multiple sits squarely in the upper-middle of that band—neither distressed nor euphoric.

Why does GD trade at $348.26 rather than $420+ despite a record $220.3 billion backlog ($270.7 billion TCV) and 12.9% Q3 revenue growth [12]? Three concrete discounts explain the price. First, Marine Systems margin (7.0% in FY25; 7.9% in Q3 26) sits 100–150 bps below its ~9% norm [10][11][12]. Sub-tier submarine bottlenecks and out-of-sequence shipyard labor continue to weigh on profitability [10][11][12]. Second, working capital absorbed $8,380 million in unbilled receivables and $9,232 million in inventories at FY25 year-end [11]. That unbilled balance includes $1.3 billion tied to one international tracked-vehicle deal [11]. Third, the U.S. market sits in a Downtrend (43.6% > 50-DMA, 8 distribution days), compressing defense multiples while CEO Phebe Novakovic hands off to Danny Deep [12].

web_blocks.takeaway: Reverse DCF shows $348.26 prices in ~5.2% 10-year revenue growth and a 10.6% terminal margin. The market gives almost zero credit for Marine margin repair toward 9%+ or Gulfstream holding 14.5%+ margins [11][12][13].

web_blocks.title: Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) Sanity Check: Gulfstream + Defense Primes
paragraphs: Valuing GD's three defense segments at a blended 13.5x forward EBIT—inline with HII and NOC—yields roughly $48B–$52B of enterprise value. Subtracting $2.6B of net debt (~$7.0B debt minus $4.4B cash at Q3 2026) leaves Aerospace priced near $47B–$51B, or ~21x EBIT [12][13]. That is fair for a 14.5%-margin franchise with 30% order growth. GD is not a deep-value bargain; upside comes from multi-year EPS and FCF compounding rather than multiple expansion.

web_blocks.html: Historical Multiple Bands & Dividend Yield Support: Across 2016–2025, GD's trailing P/E moved between ~14x and ~22x, averaging ~17.5x–18.5x forward earnings [9][13]. At $348.26 (18.43x forward P/E, 6.14% FCF yield, 1.80% dividend yield), valuation sits near its 10-year median [13]. Suppose GD compounds EPS at 9%–10% toward ~$20.75 in FY2027E and ~$22.75 in FY2028E with 100%+ FCF conversion. At a flat 19.5x multiple, shares reach $405 in 12 months. A dip to $329.18–$339.20 compresses the entry multiple to ~16.0x–16.5x FY2027E EPS, adding a real margin of safety.

Peer Multiple Spread & Implied Rerating Ceiling: Comparing GD (18.43x Forward P/E) against LMT (17.23x), NOC (18.23x), and RTX (24.07x) shows its Defense+Aerospace mix is fairly priced [13][16][17][18]. Our $405.00 Base Case target assumes zero multiple expansion (~19.5x FY27E EPS), relying instead on ~10% EPS compounding and debt paydown [13].

Margin of Safety Summary: At $348.26, GD offers ~16.3% upside to our $405 Base Case. Waiting for the $329.18–$339.20 support zone lifts Base Case upside to ~19.4%–23.0% with a 2.72:1 R:R against our $315.00 stop [13][14]. At $335.00, an investor pays roughly 16.1x FY2027E EPS and locks in nearly a 6.5% FCF yield [13]. Meanwhile, our Bear Case ($295.00) reflects 15.5x earnings if Marine stalls below 7.5% and jet orders soften [13]. Our Bull Case ($455.00) assumes Aerospace tops 15.5% margins and Marine exceeds 8.8%, lifting the multiple toward 21x [12][13].

What Changes the Valuation Call: A pullback into the $329.18–$339.20 support zone compresses the entry multiple to ~16.0x–16.5x FY2027E EPS and flips the call to an actionable buy; conversely, Marine Systems stalling below 7.5% margin or a break below $315.00 invalidates the Base Case.

book_paragraphs: Now that we have locked down the business reality in Chapters 1 through 6 without looking at a single stock quote, let us open the market ledger and ask the hardest question in investing: why is General Dynamics priced at $348.26 a share, and what future is the market already assuming?

At $348.26, you and I are looking at a $94.11 billion equity market capitalization and a $98.71 billion enterprise value. On trailing numbers, the stock trades at 20.48 times trailing earnings, 18.43 times forward earnings, 14.50 times EV/EBITDA, and 16.28 times trailing free cash flow, with a 1.80% dividend yield. If you have followed defense primes over the last two decades, those multiples will immediately feel familiar. They sit right in the upper-middle of GD's historical 15x to 21x forward P/E range. The market is neither panicking about General Dynamics nor paying a speculative AI-style premium for it.

Yet there is an obvious tension here that should make you lean forward. In Q3 2026, GD posted 12.9% revenue growth, 15.7% diluted EPS growth, and a jaw-dropping $98.8 billion in quarterly orders—lifting its total backlog to a record $220.3 billion. Why would a company with over four years of revenue sitting in funded and unfunded backlog trade at just 18.4x forward earnings, down roughly 13% from its $400 52-week high?

The answer comes down to three specific doubts that institutional investors are weighing every morning. First, Marine Systems is growing rapidly on the top line, yet its operating margin—7.0% in FY2025 and 7.9% in Q3 2026—remains stuck more than 100 basis points below its historical 9%-plus norm because of sub-tier supplier bottlenecks and out-of-sequence submarine assembly. Revenue without margin expansion is empty calories to a DCF model.

Second, working capital has been a sponge. Ending FY2025 with $8.38 billion in unbilled receivables—including $1.3 billion tied to a single international combat-vehicle contract—and $9.23 billion in inventories means cash conversion is lumpy. Investors want proof that as G700 and G800 deliveries stabilize and that international receivables milestone clears, free cash flow will consistently exceed 100% of net income.

Third, we cannot ignore the tape and the leadership transition. The broader U.S. market regime is in a confirmed Downtrend with 8 distribution days, and long-serving CEO Phebe Novakovic just presided over her final earnings call before handing the reins to Danny Deep. Wall Street almost always applies a modest 'show-me' discount during a CEO transition at an industrial compounder, even when the successor is a seasoned internal operator.

To strip away guesswork, let us run a Reverse DCF on the $348.26 stock price using an 8.5% weighted average cost of capital and a 3.0% terminal growth rate. To justify $98.71 billion in enterprise value today, GD only needs to compound revenue at roughly 5.2% per year over the next decade while holding terminal operating margins at 10.6% and converting 95% of net income into free cash flow. Think about how modest that hurdle is. GD just grew revenue 10.1% in FY2025 and 10.4% through the first nine months of 2026, its Q3 2026 operating margin already reached 10.5%, and its $220.3 billion backlog provides multi-year visibility well above 5% top-line growth.

When we line GD up against its five closest peers in the same-session snapshot, the relative pricing makes complete sense. Lockheed Martin trades at 17.23x forward earnings with a 21.31% ROIC, Northrop Grumman trades at 18.23x forward earnings with a 12.80% ROIC, and RTX trades up at 24.07x forward earnings despite an 8.22% ROIC because of its commercial aerospace aftermarket engine exposure. Meanwhile, pure-play shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls trades at 14.00x forward earnings (8.70% ROIC) and Textron sits at 11.48x (8.17% ROIC). GD's 18.43x forward P/E and 13.22% ROIC place it squarely in the sweet spot of the tier-one defense group—offering both submarine visibility and Gulfstream's high-margin private-jet cycle without RTX's richer multiple.

Even a quick Sum-of-the-Parts check confirms there is no hidden-value miracle, just solid industrial math. Value the defense segments at 13.5x forward EBIT like Northrop or HII, and Aerospace is being priced around 21x operating earnings. That is fair, not dirt cheap. So our base-case intrinsic value of $405 per share (+16.3% above $348.26) does not rely on multiple expansion—it relies on earnings compounding toward $20.50–$21.00 per share as Gulfstream margins hold 14.5%+ and Marine inches back toward 8.5%–9.0%.

Let us put that valuation math in plain English so you can see why our support zone matters so much. At today's $348.26 price, you are paying 18.43 times forward earnings for a business growing revenue at 10% and EPS at 15%+. That is already reasonable, and it explains why GD is not a broken value trap. Yet buying at 18.4x in the middle of a Stage 4 downtrend leaves less room for error if Marine Systems margins stay at 7.9% for another two quarters.

Now imagine instead that GD pulls back just 3% to 5% into our $329.18–$339.20 support zone. At $335 a share, you are paying roughly 16.1 times FY2027 estimated earnings and locking in nearly a 6.5% free cash flow yield for a company with $220.3 billion in backlog and 13.22% ROIC. That is the exact difference between paying a fair price in a falling tape and buying a premier compounder at a discount with a 2.72-to-1 reward-to-risk ratio.

That peer comparison in Chapter 7 also keeps our expectations realistic on the upside. Because GD already trades at 18.43 times forward earnings—a slight premium to Lockheed Martin at 17.23x and right in line with Northrop Grumman at 18.23x—we should not model a magical re-rating to 25x earnings. Our $405.00 Base Case target simply applies a steady 19.5x multiple to ~$20.75 of FY2027 estimated EPS, meaning earnings growth and cash generation do the heavy lifting.

Step back and look at how cleanly the valuation math aligns with our patience rule. You do not have to chase $348.26 to capture General Dynamics' multi-year compounding story. Waiting for a modest 3% to 5% pullback into the $329.18–$339.20 support zone lifts your Base Case upside to roughly 19% to 23% while cutting your downside risk to a tight, well-defined $315.00 invalidation level.

By anchoring your expectations to Reverse DCF math rather than optimistic multiple expansion, you ensure that any upside from Marine margin normalization or working-capital release works strictly in your favor.

Keeping that peer matrix and Reverse DCF table at the center of your valuation discipline prevents you from overpaying for defense headlines while highlighting the exact price zone where risk and reward tilt in your favor.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Notice how Reverse DCF protects us from storytelling. You do not need to believe in a heroic re-rating to 25x earnings for GD to work. At $348.26, the market is only pricing in 5.2% revenue growth and a 10.6% operating margin—leaving all the upside from Marine margin repair and working-capital release in your pocket if you buy at the right technical spot.
